insights.headline: You say 'I'm not a work person' in nearly the same words across 26 years, and each time you say it, the story right next to it proves the opposite.
insights.explanation: In 1999 you open with 'I don't even consider myself a work person, I want that on the record, my family is my whole entire thing' right before telling the story of the patient who made you (E1 L3). In 2005, mid-divorce, you say it again almost word for word, right after admitting the walkthrough ritual with your team is 'what I got laying around' when asked what shaped you (E2 L52-57). In 2025 you're still saying it — 'my family is the priority, period, it always has been, I'm not one of these people that's married to a hospital' — right after describing arriving two and a half hours late to your son's birthday because you stayed for a colleague in a parking deck (E5 L51, L46). The claim hasn't moved in 26 years. The evidence against it has only piled up.

evidence.quote: I don't even consider myself a work person, I want that on the record, my family is my whole entire thing, always has been.
My family is the priority, period, it always has been, I'm not one of these people that's married to a hospital.

insights.would_predict: If you tracked a normal week's time and emotional bandwidth honestly, work would consume more of it than family, even on weeks you'd call unremarkable.

insights.headline: You override authority figures' explicit clinical calls every single time your read of the situation disagrees with theirs, and you're willing to take the professional hit for it.
insights.explanation: In 1999 a resident tells you to 'go sit down' — you sit for ninety seconds and act anyway (E1 L29-34). In 2005 a fellow questions whether you should even be the one calling it, in front of the attending, after you'd already pushed your clinical read (E2 L32-33). In 2020 an administrator tells you to 'trust the process' and your team later calls you 'rigid' for isolating a patient anyway (E4 L27-29). In 2025 you ask a physician for more resuscitation time past his stated stopping point (E5 L34-36). Four different types of authority, 26 years, same response each time — this reads as a stable operating stance, not a one-off.

evidence.quote: he says, "She's anxious. Everybody in this hallway is anxious. Go sit down for a minute, you look tired."
the word they used was rigid

insights.would_predict: In a non-clinical dispute — a school meeting, a contractor disagreement — you'll refuse to defer to credentialed authority once you believe you have the better read of the facts.

insights.headline: Under the worst pressure in the room, your instinct is to narrate your own reasoning out loud to whoever's junior, turning crisis into someone else's training.
insights.explanation: This shows up almost identically 26 years apart: in 1999 with Nicole ('I'm talking the whole time to the girl who was orienting with me... you're gonna see this again,' E1 L46) and in 2025 with Brianna, where you name it directly as a technique — 'that's a trick... it works on anybody' — that has since spread to Brianna's own patients (E5 L19-21, L27). Same behavior, decades apart, now with visible downstream impact on someone else's practice.

evidence.quote: Because if you're teaching it you're not shaking. That's just — that's just efficient.
I don't care what they scored. You talk to 'em.

insights.would_predict: You'll keep gravitating toward informal mentoring without needing a title for it, and junior colleagues will remember you less for your clinical calls than for how you talked them through the worst moments.

insights.headline: You talk directly to the dying and the effectively-dead even though you say flatly they can't hear you — and you can't explain why you keep doing it.
insights.explanation: With the motorcycle patient you wash his face and apologize 'probably forty times' while insisting 'I know he can't hear me... I'm not out here being mystical' (E3 L23-27). With the drowned child you narrate comfort — 'I'm sorry it's so cold in here' — to a body starved of oxygen, and frame it as something you teach rather than something private ('you talk to 'em,' E5 L23-25). Both times you call it procedural or pragmatic, yet it costs you time you don't strictly need to spend, and when asked directly why, you land on 'Isn't that — I don't know' (E3 L48). You're doing something you can't name a reason for, twice, a decade apart.

insights.headline: When something devastating happens, you describe the aftermath through small domestic images — a driveway, a bowl of cereal, a cold garage — almost never through a direct statement of feeling.
insights.explanation: After the ruptured ectopic, you don't say you were shaken — you say you sat in the driveway 'for like fifteen minutes... Just sitting' (E1 L55-56). After the 18-year-old's death, mid-divorce, you don't describe grief — you say you 'sat on the floor of the kitchen and ate a bowl of cereal at like eight in the morning with the blinds closed' (E2 L51). During COVID, six weeks of undressing in a cold garage to avoid touching your kids stands in for whatever you felt about the risk (E4 L42). The pattern holds across every account of something devastating — it reads as a reporting style, not an absence of feeling.

insights.headline: The people you call 'good' — your mother, Dre — are consistently the ones absorbing childcare during your highest-stakes work moments, which raises the question of whether your 'family first' claim only holds because someone else is covering the gap.
insights.explanation: In 1999 your mother has baby Jaylen while you're dealing with the hemorrhaging patient (E1 L55). You don't name this as a debt, but it recurs as the structural condition underneath the 'family first' claim.

insights.would_predict: If asked directly about your marriage's division of labor, you'll minimize your own dependence on Dre's caregiving and frame your work absences as exceptions rather than a standing arrangement he enables.

insights.headline: You keep turning down the role that would let you stop absorbing the worst cases yourself — and when you finally take it, you use it to take on more of the worst cases, not fewer.
insights.explanation: You 'kept turning down charge... they asked me like three times' before 2014 (E3 L3-5), and only take it in 2020 for a defensive reason — to protect the department from a scared charge nurse — then immediately undercut the position's purpose by taking the highest-risk assignment yourself instead of floating (E4 L3-21). facts.what_happened: In 2014, speaker had just moved to south campus, was not yet charge nurse, had been asked to take charge role about three times and turned it down.
A 22-year-old man came in on a Sunday after a motorcycle accident, no helmet, field condition described as bad.
A head bleed was visible on the scout film.
Neuro was called and was coming from downtown; the patient's family was in Rockdale County trying to get there.
Staff determined within the first ten minutes that the patient was not going to survive/recover.
The room emptied out at a certain point.
The room emptied because there was nothing more to do for this patient, while fourteen other patients in the department needed care.
Speaker told their tech to go help Ronda in room twelve.
Speaker was left alone with the patient.
Speaker cleaned the patient.

Speaker said sorry approximately forty times.
Speaker states she knows what a GCS of three is.
The patient's mother arrived and asked if he said anything; speaker told her no, but that he wasn't by himself.
Speaker finished her shift.
Speaker arrived home; Dre had fed the kids.
Malachi was three or four years old; Kiana was approximately ten or eleven.
The kids wanted speaker to watch a show with them, and she watched it.
Speaker did not say anything about her day.
Speaker's sister Cheryl called that week; the two had had a falling out about their mother's house.
Speaker saw Cheryl's name on the phone and let the call go to voicemail.
Speaker and Cheryl still talk to this day and see each other at Thanksgiving, but never discussed the falling out again.

facts.what_happened: In March 2020 speaker became charge nurse.
Debra left the charge position; a replacement nurse was put in who was described as good and smart but scared.
Speaker said 'Give it to me,' taking on the charge role.
Rooms 17 and 18 were negative pressure rooms where all suspected COVID cases were sent.
An administrator from the third floor came down and said staff needed to 'be mindful of utilization' on N95 masks.
Policy stated one N95 mask per nurse per shift.
Speaker told the administrator nurses were entering that room eleven or twelve times a shift.
Administrator responded they were 'looking at clustering care.'
Administrator said, "Yolanda, I need you to trust the process," and speaker said okay.
Speaker took over patient assignment for rooms 17 and 18 herself.
Speaker did this every shift.
This continued for about six weeks.
In May, a patient in room 18 was classified by others as a low-suspicion rule-out, there for a hip issue.
Speaker said to put her in the negative pressure room.
The patient tested positive two days later after being moved to the ortho floor, and four staff members on that floor were infected.
One infected staff member was Miss Gwen from environmental services, age 68.
Miss Gwen was on a ventilator for nineteen days.
No one from administration said anything to the speaker about the outcome.
Speaker's son Jaylen was grown and living in Columbus at the time.
Daughter Kiana was doing school on a computer at the kitchen table; son Dre was home because his shop was closed.
Speaker undressed in the garage nightly, placed scrubs in a bag, and went directly to the shower without contact with family.
Speaker did not hug her children for six weeks.
Dre told speaker, "You could take a leave. They got leave."
Speaker responded by asking who would take rooms 17 and 18.
Dre looked at speaker and went to bed.
Speaker states she does not pursue management track, does her shifts, and goes home.
